oil.summary: Crude markets whipsawed violently on Friday, with Brent shedding 8.85% to $97.17/bbl and WTI falling 2.54% to $92.20/bbl, widening the Brent-WTI spread to roughly $12 — a dislocation driven by soaring freight costs and Hormuz-related supply fears hitting waterborne Brent grades harder. RBOB gasoline led the selloff with a brutal 10.85% drop, while heating oil fell 6.33%. The catalyst for the late-session giveback was a reported Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the US meets conditions, easing near-term blockade fears. Offsetting that relief: Iran's oil blockade remains active, Saudi Aramco is still recovering from pipeline attacks, and Trump's threat to escalate strikes adds tail risk. The US temporarily easing Russia oil sanctions to cap prices drew pushback from European allies. India confirmed it will continue diesel exports to ease the global fuel crunch.
drivers: Iran's conditional 7-day Hormuz reopening offer triggered a sharp price selloff, unwinding war-premium bids across crude and products
Brent-WTI spread blew out to ~$12 on elevated freight costs and supply disruption fears concentrated in waterborne Middle Eastern grades
Geopolitical cross-currents remain intense: US eases Russia sanctions temporarily, Trump threatens to escalate Iran strikes, and Saudi Aramco Petroline only partially restored after attacks

gas.summary: Natural gas markets pulled back on both sides of the Atlantic, with TTF falling 4.03% to €72.08/MWh and Henry Hub easing 2.37% to $3.218/MMBtu, though both remain sharply higher on a one-month basis — up 9.83% and 13.27% respectively. The TTF retreat was likely tied to the broader risk-off tone in energy following Hormuz diplomacy hopes, though the EU's Gas Coordination Group separately signalled supply remains stable despite low storage levels. The Netherlands publicly challenged the bloc's gas storage mandate, calling it fiscally burdensome after a €1.14 billion bill. On the supply side, Baker Hughes data showed the US oil and gas rig count rose this week, and BP is reportedly eyeing Devon Energy's Eagle Ford assets as CEO Meg O'Neill pivots the company back toward hydrocarbons.
drivers: TTF and Henry Hub both retreated as Hormuz diplomatic progress reduced immediate supply-shock premia built in over the prior week
EU storage mandate under political pressure: Netherlands seeking to scrap the system after a $1.14 billion fiscal hit, even as the Gas Coordination Group downplays supply risk
US upstream activity picking up — Baker Hughes rig count rose this week, and BP is evaluating shale acquisitions, signalling longer-term supply confidence

power.summary: EU carbon allowances (EUA) bucked the broader energy selloff, edging up 1.10% to $82.625/EUA, extending a steady one-month gain of 3.23%. The relative resilience of carbon pricing contrasts with sharply lower TTF gas — down 4.03% on the day — which in theory reduces the cost of gas-fired generation and can soften short-term EUA demand. However, geopolitical uncertainty and structural supply tightness appear to be supporting the carbon floor. In the broader power complex, India is weighing mandatory imported coal blending at domestic power plants after coal stocks at many facilities deteriorated due to logistics failures, a development that could lift seaborne thermal coal demand. The Netherlands' push to scrap EU gas storage targets and Trump's diesel export threat add further stress to European energy security heading into winter. Headline data for power generation prices themselves is limited today.
drivers: EUAs held firm at $82.63 despite a sharp TTF gas drop, suggesting structural carbon support is outweighing short-term fuel-switching signals
India considering mandatory imported coal blending at power plants amid crumbling domestic coal stocks — potential upside for seaborne thermal coal demand
European energy security under twin pressure: Netherlands challenging the EU gas storage mandate while Iran's Hormuz proposal keeps winter supply risk elevated
